questions.q: What level does a data policy operate at?
options: A single employee's personal task list
The precise encryption algorithm an application must use
The exact technical configuration of a database table
High-level vision and direction — what is required and why, not how to implement it
questions.explain: Policies state the rule and reasoning; the implementation detail belongs to standards, covered in the next lesson.

questions.q: In the example policy statement — 'customer financial information may only be accessed on a need-to-know basis' — what is deliberately left out?
options: The specific technical controls (encryption, access process) that implement the rule
Who the rule applies to
Whether the information is confidential at all
The reasoning behind the rule
questions.explain: Policies state the rule and the 'why' while staying implementation-agnostic; technical implementation belongs to a standard.

questions.q: According to this lesson, who typically proposes a new data policy for a domain?
options: The data owner, since they hold the business context and Accountable role
A random employee selected by lottery
The data consumer, since they use the data most often
The external regulator directly
questions.explain: The owner holds business context and accountability for the domain, making them the natural source of a proposed policy.

questions.q: Who, per this lesson, typically gives a data policy its formal, cross-domain approval?
options: Only an external auditor, never anyone inside the company
The governance committee
A policy never needs formal approval to be real
Any individual employee who happens to read it
questions.explain: The governance committee (Chapter 3, Lesson 16) is the body set up specifically to approve policy, especially anything crossing domains.

questions.q: Why does a policy that mandates a specific tool or technique tend to 'age badly'?
options: Because tools never actually change once a policy names them
Because policies are legally required to be rewritten every single week
Because standards are not allowed to mention any tool at all, ever
Because tools and techniques change, while a good policy's underlying rule and reasoning should stay stable
questions.explain: Keeping implementation detail out of the policy and inside standards/procedures means the policy doesn't need rewriting every time a tool changes.
